title: Judicial Pronouncements on Separation of Powers

content.overview: Indian judicial pronouncements have shaped the doctrine of separation of powers by rejecting rigid separation, affirming checks and balances, protecting essential judicial functions, and locating separation within the basic structure.
content.glance: State the proposition from the leading cases already in the topic file; apply the functional Indian approach; avoid rigid tripartite slogans.
content.study: Case law establishes that the Indian Constitution does not embody a rigid separation of powers. Executive action may extend to matters not covered by legislation within constitutional limits; judicial functions cannot be usurped; and the essential features of separation form part of the basic structure. Use authorities already present in the file for the propositions they actually support; verification of precise holdings remains a separate gate. Current-law framing: ground the analysis in the Constitution and decided cases. Do not treat BSA 2023 as the source of this doctrine.

sections.heading: Rejection of Rigid Separation
sections.body: Indian authorities treat separation as functional, not rigid.

sections.heading: Executive and Legislative Spheres
sections.body: Executive power is wide but not unlimited; it remains subject to the Constitution and law.

sections.heading: Protection of Judicial Function
sections.body: Essential adjudicatory functions cannot be transferred in a manner that destroys judicial independence.

sections.heading: Basic Structure Link
sections.body: Essential separation features are part of the basic structure.

sections.heading: Method
sections.body: Read each authority for its actual proposition; do not invent holdings.

examples.title: Ram Jawaya proposition
examples.body: On problem facts involving executive action without prior legislation, apply the functional separation approach associated with Ram Jawaya Kapur rather than rigid separation slogans.

examples.title: Basic structure link
examples.body: Where a measure threatens essential separation features, basic-structure analysis associated with Kesavananda is engaged.

hypotheticals.question: Does every case citing separation freeze all administrative power?
hypotheticals.analysis: Cases calibrate functions; they do not abolish administration.

hypotheticals.question: Does basic structure mean no delegated legislation?
hypotheticals.analysis: Delegated legislation is permitted within constitutional limits.

cases.name: Ram Jawaya Kapur v State of Punjab
cases.facts: Executive action and constitutional distribution of governmental functions.
cases.issue: Whether the Indian Constitution adopts a rigid separation of powers.
cases.ratioDecidendi: The Constitution does not impose separation in absolute rigidity; functions are sufficiently differentiated.
cases.relevance: Leading case on rejection of rigid separation.

cases.name: Asif Hameed v State of Jammu and Kashmir
cases.facts: Limits of judicial intervention in matters allocated to other organs.
cases.ratioDecidendi: Each constitutional organ must operate within its assigned sphere.

cases.name: Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala
cases.issue: Whether separation of powers forms part of the constitutional structure.
cases.ratioDecidendi: Checks and balances and separation of powers are components of the basic structure.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should a separation case-law problem be analysed?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: I. Identify relevant case proposition. II. Apply functional separation standard. III. Address basic structure if engaged. IV. Conclude without inventing holdings.

questionsAndAnswers.question: What should submissions contain?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Case propositions from the file; functional standard; precise relief.
